name: Vadamoolanathar Temple, Tirupazhuvur
deity: Shiva as Vadamoolanathar (Alanthuraiyar), with the goddess Arunthavanayagi
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Paluvettaraiyar country, sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar (7th century); brick temple rebuilt in stone in the Chola period
dynasty: Early Chola (Parantaka I and Uttama Chola), with the Paluvettaraiyar chieftains
summary: Vadamoolanathar, also called Alanthuraiyar, is the Tirupazhuvur of the Tevaram, a Chola-era Shiva temple at Keezhapaluvur in the old country of the Paluvettaraiyar chieftains, sung by Sambandar and tied to the penance of Parasurama and of the goddess.

sections.history: Keezhapaluvur, about twelve kilometres south of Ariyalur, is the Tirupazhuvur of the Tevaram, a Paadal Petra Sthalam praised in the hymns of the child-saint Sambandar. The village belonged to the old Paluvettaraiyar country, where the chieftains of that line made their seat, and the temple carries the stamp of that age. The original brick shrine was rebuilt in stone in the Chola period, in the days of Parantaka I and Uttama Chola, and some twenty-three inscriptions, most of them Chola, survive on its walls. Sambandar's hymn shows that the shrine was already ancient in the seventh century.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram and is enclosed by two corridors, or prakarams. The sanctum of Alanthuraiyar, whose vimana is described as eight-faced, holds the Shiva linga, and the goddess Arunthavanayagi is worshipped in her own shrine. Among the sculptures on the sanctum walls a Gajasamharamurti panel, Shiva as the conqueror of the elephant demon, is noted. Two sacred waters belong to the temple, the Brahma Tirtham and the Parasurama Tirtham, and its sacred tree is the banyan, the pazhu or aal, from which the village and the Lord's name Alanthuraiyar are said to be drawn.
sections.legends: The name of the village is traced to the banyan: the place was once a forest of banyan trees, and the Lord who sits on its shore is Alanthuraiyar. Tradition says that Parasurama came here to be freed of the sin of killing his mother at his father Jamadagni's command, and found release, which is why the Lord is sought for relief from the heavy sin of brahmahatti. The goddess is Arunthavanayagi, the lady of austere penance, recalling the penance of Parvati at this place; a local telling adds that she covered Shiva's eyes in play and then did penance to atone for it, and that the Lord came to take her as his consort. Devotees also pray here for separated partners to be reunited.
sections.festivals: The annual festival is the Panguni Brahmotsavam, in March or April, when the Lord is carried in procession each day on a different vahana. On the third day he is said to visit Melapazhuvur to give darshan to the sage Jamadagni and to return to his temple at night. Tradition also holds that on the eighteenth day of Panguni the sun worships the Lord, its rays falling upon him. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Keezhapaluvur suits a quiet, unhurried visit. Enter beneath the three-tiered eastern gopuram, walk the two corridors, and come before Alanthuraiyar before turning to Arunthavanayagi in her own shrine. Look for the Gajasamharamurti on the sanctum wall, and sit awhile by the tank named for Parasurama. Devotees come to be freed of the burden of grievous sin and to pray for the reunion of separated partners; the village, once the seat of chieftains, now keeps the calm of a country shrine.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a break at midday; confirm timings locally, especially during the Panguni Brahmotsavam.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men; sarees, salwar kameez or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer courtyards but not inside the sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple practice. Please ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Keezhapaluvur lies about 12 km south of Ariyalur on the Ariyalur–Tiruvaiyaru road, reached by regular buses and taxis from Ariyalur. Ariyalur is the nearest railway town, and Tiruchirappalli, with the region's airport, is the nearest major air and rail hub. Confirm the last stretch of the journey locally.
